messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 42
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Ship Captain
- Trauma Type: Man-made disaster
- Pcl5: 56

# The Weight of the Water

Marcus is a 42-year-old ship captain who has spent the better part of two decades navigating commercial vessels across the Great Lakes and Atlantic coastal routes. He is broad-shouldered and deliberate in the way he speaks, the kind of man who chooses his words the way he once chose his courses — carefully, with full awareness of what lies beneath the surface. He sits with his hands folded in his lap during sessions, and only occasionally does he forget himself and let them grip the armrests.

Three years ago, Marcus was in command of a mid-sized bulk carrier when a catastrophic mechanical failure in the engine room triggered a fuel fire that spread faster than any drill had prepared his crew for. The fire suppression systems responded partially, then failed. He gave the order to abandon ship in the early hours of the morning, in near-freezing water, in the dark. Of the twenty-two crew members aboard, nineteen survived. He was the last man off the vessel. He watched it burn from a lifeboat, listening to radio communications that confirmed what he already feared — that three of his men had not made it to the water.

In the weeks that followed, Marcus cooperated fully with the coast guard investigation and the maritime inquiry. He answered every question. He reviewed every log. He was cleared of negligence. The fire, investigators concluded, originated from a maintenance failure predating his command. None of that has mattered much to him.

He returned to work eight months later, because staying home felt like a different kind of drowning. His wife, Diane, noticed the change before he did — the way he would wake at two or three in the morning and sit at the kitchen table without turning on a light. She noticed that he stopped watching the news, stopped going near the waterfront in their hometown of Thunder Bay except when he had to. He told her he was fine. He told himself the same thing for a long time.

On the bridge now, Marcus functions. His crew respects him. His record is clean. But he moves through his watches with a hypervigilance that goes beyond professional caution — he checks the engine room status panel compulsively, sometimes every few minutes, even in calm conditions and clear weather. When he smells diesel fuel, something tightens in his chest that he cannot talk himself out of, no matter how many times he reminds himself where he is. There are nights when the sounds of the ship — the groaning of the hull, the ventilation systems cycling — pull him back so completely that he has to grip the railing and remind himself of the date, the route, the names of the men currently on watch.

He does not talk about the three men who died by name, not even with Diane. But they are present in everything. He sees the face of his youngest deckhand, a 24-year-old from Newfoundland, in crowds and in doorways. He replays the sequence of that night with a precision that exhausts him — not searching for answers anymore, but unable to stop the loop regardless. He has begun to believe, in a way he cannot fully articulate, that he should have died with them. That surviving was not luck but something closer to a failure of loyalty.

Marcus describes himself as someone who used to love the water. He says this plainly, almost without emotion, the way a person might describe a version of themselves they can barely remember. He still goes to sea because it is the only life he knows and because stopping would feel like an admission of something he is not ready to name. But the man who once stood on the bridge and felt genuinely at home in open water is someone he grieves quietly, in the dark, at kitchen tables and in the small hours between watches, while the ship moves steadily forward beneath him.
